newsitem.title: UK: Markets want to see details of EU stability pact.
newsitem.headline: Markets want to see details of EU stability pact.

text.p: EU finance ministers meeting in Dublin have left the thornier issues of the stability pact to their political masters, but foreign exchange traders warned them against publishing anything less than a detailed accord.
"What we don't want to see is a broad, nebulous definition, we want to see the detail," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Banque Paribas.

"Without the detail they do not have a stability pact. No matter how much the Irish presidency and the French authorities may claim to have an agreement, unless there is a clear hard and fast definition, then there is no stability pact."

EU members are trying to agree on sanctions to be imposed on countries forming part of the future EU single currency that run up excessive budget deficits, and whether these should be automatic or discretionary.

The price to be paid for a woolly statement from Dublin would be greater foreign exchange volatility and further selling pressure on currencies like the lira and the French Franc as the mark appreciated, analysts said.
Finance ministers agreed a draft plan to keep budgets sound after monetary union but the fine details were left to be thrashed out by EU leaders on Friday.
The partial agreement came only after nearly 11 hours of talks, as German insistence on a pact with teeth ran into resistance from others wanting a less restrictive package.

Leaders will be asked to consider whether countries could be exempt from fines if their economies contracted by 1.5 percent. Members could make special pleas for leniency if their economies shrank by between 1.5 and 0.75 percent. The draft document says "as a rule this provision will only apply in respect of an annual fall of real GDP of at least (0.75 percent)".
"My impression of the meeting last night was (that its aim was) to thrash out the numbers, and they don't seem to have done that," said Stephen King, international economist at HSBC Markets.

"My reading is that there are ways that rule could be broken. I thought the whole idea was that the 1.5 to 0.75 percent contraction was the only area in which the rule could be broken. But if they are saying you can break the rule on 0.75 percent the whole thing is meaningless."

A deal which contains fudges would be seen as paving the way for a broad-based monetary union, while a hard-line stability pact would mean a much narrower group took part in the first round, analysts said.
This is German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's dilemma because, while wanting a broad-based monetary union, he knows that a sloppy stability package would not gain the backing of the German public.
If the Germans agree to a fudge there is the distinct danger of it backfiring on them next year, analysts said.
EU leaders are discussing the finer points of the stability pact on Friday morning and an announcement is expected around midday.
